title: Franklin Street Looks Reborn. Look Closer and It's Two Different Streets.
summary: Explore what's changing on Franklin Street in Chapel Hill in 2026, including restaurant openings, vacant spaces, ownership patterns, and district shifts.
body_markdown:
Sometime this week, the Orange County Sheriff's Office padlocked Breadman's, the longtime Chapel Hill bakery that had been fighting a rent dispute with its landlord. A few blocks away, a sign went up announcing that a 7 Brew Coffee Shop is moving into the storefront Starbucks moved out of last year, right next to Raising Cane's. Both things are true at the same time, on the same street, in the same month. Recent roundups of new restaurants on Franklin Street capture one part of a changing mix of openings, relocations and closures.


## New restaurant openings on Franklin Street


Walk Franklin Street this August and the new signage tells a genuinely interesting story about what Chapel Hill wants to eat. Géos Tavern & Oyster Bar opened June 8 at East 54, bringing North Carolina seafood and a 220-seat dining room from the team behind Giorgios Hospitality Group. Good Fortune, a cocktail bar, is now open on West Franklin. Kolapasi Indian Canteen, a South Indian fast-casual chain, opened its second North Carolina location on West Franklin. Próximo, a Spanish tapas and wine bar built around chef Brandon Sharp's cooking from Hawthorne & Wood and Bluebird, has been serving crispy sea bass and seared meatballs on East Franklin since September 2024. The Latin Effect, which started as a food truck in 2020, now has a permanent home on West Franklin serving Honduran and Central American dishes like catrachitas and pupusas. Road to Myanmar has brought Burmese, Thai, and Malaysian cooking to East Franklin as well.


None of this reads like a street in decline. It reads like a street getting more interesting, one small independent lease at a time.


## The one who's actually buying the buildings


Here's the part that doesn't show up in the "new restaurants" lists. When Raising Cane's arrived on Franklin Street, it didn't just sign a lease. It bought the whole building, including the retail space Starbucks used to occupy. Starbucks didn't close. It relocated across the street into something bigger. A report by[Downtown Chapel Hill](https://www.downtownchapelhill.com/new-restaurants-come-to-franklin-street) quoted Jeri Lynn Schulke, executive director of the Chapel Hill Downtown Partnership, saying "everybody in our town was hoping that somebody would come along" to fill those long-empty corners.


That relief is real. Empty storefronts at Franklin and Columbia had been a visible wound for years. But the fix came from a national chain with the capital to purchase real estate outright, not lease it. Now the pattern is repeating in smaller ways. Construction began in July on a shared Jimmy John's and Baskin-Robbins location, taking over a long-vacant lot between the Target and the Panera on West Franklin. Zaxbys opened on East Franklin in March 2025. 7 Brew is filling the space Starbucks left behind. None of these are villains. They're simply a different kind of tenant than the ones filling the storefronts one block over, and they're arriving with a different kind of financial backing.


## Recent closures alongside new openings


Linda's Bar & Grill, a Chapel Hill fixture for years, closed in January 2025 citing lost revenue and staffing problems it couldn't solve. Ram's Corner, a sports bar that opened on West Franklin in October 2025 with ping pong tables and a front porch built for game nights, had already closed by the time trade listings were checked again this year, less than a full year after its debut. Breadman's, a longtime Chapel Hill bakery, is now padlocked over a rent dispute with its landlord, its future genuinely uncertain as of this writing.


Every one of these closures happened for its own reason. The property purchase that brought in Raising Cane's is another part of Franklin Street's recent change. Franklin Street isn't choosing between decline and revival. It's running both processes at once.


## Different kinds of storefront openings


This is worth sitting with if you live here, because it changes what a "new restaurant opened" headline actually tells you. A new Burmese restaurant or a Honduran food truck's first permanent home is a story about somebody opening a restaurant in a storefront. A Jimmy John's and Baskin-Robbins opening in a lot that's sat empty for years is a story about a larger operator developing a long-vacant lot. Both make the street feel busier, though they do so through different kinds of openings.


The independent wave and the corporate wave are both genuinely happening on Franklin Street right now, in the same eight or nine blocks, sometimes in storefronts next door to each other. Mediterranean Deli reopened last year with a larger, more expansive layout after a two-year closure following a fire, proof that the street's older institutions can still come back stronger. The Yogurt Pump, owned by UNC alumni Jim and Susan Kitchen, is still there. That kind of staying power sits a few doors down from a building a national chain just purchased outright. Both are real. Neither cancels the other out.


## What this actually means if you're walking the street this month


If you're trying to make sense of what's new, the useful move isn't to treat every opening as equally telling. Notice which openings use existing storefronts, and which involve developing sites. Yeti Bowl and Shakes is set to take over the old Hibachi & Company space on East Franklin, a smaller-scale transition worth watching for what comes next. Naan by Gulshan is still waiting on final inspections before it can open its doors, another small operator preparing to open.


Each opening, relocation and closure has its own context. For a particular storefront, it can be useful to ask who owns the building and what business occupied it before.
